title: The LORD on Trial Against the Nations' Gods
summary: God summons the nations to court and asks who has raised up a conqueror from the east, answering that he, the first and the last, has done it. While the nations bolster their idols, God turns to Israel, his chosen servant, and tells the worm of Jacob not to fear, for he will help them and turn the desert into springs. The chapter closes with a second trial scene in which the idols are challenged to predict the future and are exposed as nothing.
story: Chapter 40 told the exiles that God was coming and that no one could be compared with him. Chapter 41 puts that claim to a public test. A world power is rising in the east, and the nations are frightened. Who is behind it? The chapter answers that the LORD is, and that the purpose of the upheaval is the good of his servant Israel. Here the word “servant” appears for the first time in this part of the book, applied to the whole people. It will be one of the key words of chapters 41 to 53, and the reader should watch how its meaning grows.
historical:
The conqueror “from the east” (verse 2) and “from the north” (verse 25) is not named until 44:28, but nearly all interpreters identify him as Cyrus the Great, the Persian king whose armies swept through the Near East in the mid-sixth century BC. Cyrus defeated the Medes around 550 BC, conquered the wealthy kingdom of Lydia in Asia Minor in the 540s, and took Babylon in 539 BC. Persia lay to the east of Babylon, and his campaigns reached Babylonia from the north as well, which may explain the two directions. For the exiles, his rise was the political event that might mean either new terror or release.

On the traditional reading of Isaiah's authorship, these verses foresee Cyrus long before his birth; on the view that chapters 40 to 55 come from the exile, they interpret his campaigns as they were happening. Either way, the chapter's claim is the same: the one who announces events beforehand is the true God.
cultural:
The trial scenes draw on the ancient practice of settling disputes at the city gate, where both sides presented their case, called witnesses, and waited for judgment. Here God is both a party and the judge, and the nations and their gods are summoned to defend themselves. The test proposed is prediction: gods who cannot say what will happen, or explain what has happened, are not gods at all. In Babylon, divination was a serious and learned business, with experts reading omens in the livers of sacrificed animals and in the movements of the stars to discern the will of the gods. The chapter's challenge strikes at that whole system.

Verses 6 and 7 give a satirical picture of idol-making under pressure: frightened craftsmen encourage one another, check the soldering, and nail the statue down so it will not fall over. The picture of Israel as a threshing sledge (verse 15) comes from farming. Such sledges were heavy boards set with sharp stones or iron teeth underneath, dragged over grain to break the husks. The weak “worm of Jacob” becomes an instrument that levels mountains.
literary: The chapter alternates between two kinds of speech. Trial speeches (verses 1 to 7 and 21 to 29) summon the nations and their gods, pose questions, and deliver a verdict. Between them stand oracles of salvation (verses 8 to 13, 14 to 16, and 17 to 20), a form built around the phrase “Do not fear” followed by God's reason for the command and his promise to act. The contrast is deliberate: the nations comfort each other and fasten their idols so they will not topple, while Israel is held by the right hand of God, who says “I will uphold you.” The chapter ends on emptiness: the idols are “as empty as the wind.”

outline.t: The nations summoned: who raised up the conqueror?
The frightened nations shore up their idols
Israel, God's chosen servant: do not fear
The worm of Jacob made a threshing sledge
Water in the desert for the poor and needy
The idols challenged to predict and found empty

doctrines.note: God claims the rise of a world conqueror as his own work: “I, the LORD—the first and the last— I am He.” History is not a contest among nations and their gods but the unfolding of the purposes of the one God.
Israel's standing as God's servant rests on his choice and his promise to Abraham, whom he calls “My friend.” The exiles who feared they had been discarded hear, “I have chosen and not rejected you.”
The idols fail the test of speaking and acting in history. The chapter's judgment is blunt: “you are nothing and your work is of no value.”

words.note: Eved, servant or slave. Being God's servant is a title of honor and belonging, used of Abraham, Moses, and David. Here it names the people of Israel (verses 8 and 9), chosen and upheld by God. In the next chapter the same word introduces a figure whose identity is debated, so this first use sets the stage.

Ga'al, to redeem, from which comes go'el, the redeemer. In Israelite family law the go'el was the close relative who bought back land, freed a kinsman from debt slavery, or avenged a death. When God calls himself Israel's Redeemer, he claims them as family and takes responsibility for their release.

Bachar, to choose. Election in the Old Testament is God's free choice of a people for relationship and for a purpose. The chapter pairs choosing with not rejecting, speaking directly to exiles who feared that the exile meant God had cast them off.

Nagad, to tell or declare. It is the key verb of the trial in verses 22 to 26: the gods are challenged to declare what will happen. The LORD's claim is that he alone has declared it beforehand, and this becomes a running argument through chapter 48.

christ: Several threads of the chapter reappear in the New Testament. The title “the first and the last” (verse 4, and again in 44:6 and 48:12) is taken up in Revelation, where the risen Jesus speaks it of himself (Revelation 1:17; 22:13), a striking claim to share the identity of Israel's one God. The words “I am He” echo in Jesus's sayings in John's Gospel (for example John 13:19), where he tells his disciples that he is telling them beforehand so that when it happens they will believe that he is the one, the same argument from prediction made in this chapter. Mary's song in Luke 1:54 praises God for helping his servant Israel, language that recalls this chapter. And the servant theme introduced here, first applied to the whole nation, will narrow in the chapters ahead toward the figure the New Testament identifies with Jesus.

hard.q: The chapter mocks the idols as nothing. Is it fair to the religions of Israel's neighbors?
hard.a: Ancient worshipers in Babylon did not believe the statue was simply the god. They held that the deity was present in the image after it had been ritually consecrated, much as a king was present through his representatives. So a modern reader may wonder whether Isaiah's satire of carpenters and goldsmiths misses the point. Many scholars respond that Isaiah knew exactly what worshipers believed and was attacking the claim at its root: if the gods are real, let them act and speak in history. The satire targets the dependence of those gods on human hands, precisely the thing a consecrated image could not escape. Others note that the chapter's main argument is not the manufacture of idols but their silence, and that argument is directed at claims, not at people. The prophet's harshest words, notably, are spoken to Israel's own leaders elsewhere in the book, and the invitation extended to the nations later in these chapters (45:22) shows the goal is not scorn but conversion.

questions: God says “Do not fear” three times in this chapter. What reasons does he give, and which one speaks most to your fears?
The chapter calls Israel a “worm” and then a threshing sledge. How does God's strength relate to his people's weakness here?
The idols are tested by whether they can speak and act. What are the modern equivalents of gods that promise much and can do nothing?
